## Overview

The vignette on maps between models used small examples written for the
purpose. This one tries the same ideas on the published models of
EcologicalCellularAutomata, where the rules were written for other reasons and
much of the dynamics lives outside them. Several relations turn out to hold
exactly, and the attempt shows what a map of models cannot see.

A map of models compares rules, but a zoo problem is more than its rule: it may
have covariates, kernel fields and callbacks acting on the whole lattice. So
there are two checks. `is_model_map(f)` tests the rules on local configurations.
`is_model_map(f, prob)` runs both models on one problem and compares every saved
state exactly, and is the only one that sees the rest. Its `true` holds for
that problem.

This is a **research extension**, beyond the papers the package implements. The
package does not depend on the zoo; only this vignette loads it.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CategoricalCellularAutomata
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore: CellularAutomataCore, CAProblem, solve, remake, Torus, Margolus
using Catlab: codom
using Plots
```

## Forgetting what a model only records

The *Tuta absoluta* model follows the leafminer's spread across Asia on monthly
climate data [@Guimapi2020]. Each land cell is susceptible, exposed or invaded,
and two more layers record the months it was first reached and invaded.
`forget_layers` builds the model without them from the same rule, so no second
copy of the rule can drift from the first. Whether the result is a map is a
real question, answered here by running 300 months over the real climate:

```{julia}
tuta = build(:tuta_absoluta_asia)
plain_tuta = forget_layers(tuta, :reached, :invaded)
tprob = problem(:tuta_absoluta_asia)
(codomain=codom(plain_tuta).name, months=tprob.tspan[2],
 is_model_map=is_model_map(plain_tuta, tprob),
 land_can_be_forgotten=is_model_map(forget_layers(tuta, :land), tprob))
```

The records add nothing to the dynamics, only a history that the smaller model
cannot give: the figure sets the month each cell was reached beside the stage
that the smaller model holds at the end. Forgetting `land` instead is not a map, since
the rule reads it.

```{julia}
u = solve(tprob).u[end]
small = pushforward(plain_tuta, u)
northup(a) = reverse(a; dims=1)
plot(heatmap(northup(map(x -> x < 0 ? NaN : Float64(x), u.reached)); c=:viridis,
             title="full model: month first reached", titlefontsize=10),
     heatmap(northup(map((s, l) -> l ? Float64(s) : NaN, small.state, small.land));
             c=:viridis, colorbar=false, clims=(0, 2),
             title="without the records, month 300: purple S, green E, yellow I",
             titlefontsize=10);
     layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 300), ticks=false, framestyle=:box)
```

## A management model and its base model

The management model of the emerald ash borer [@Mercader2011b] extends the
base model [@Mercader2011] with two layers and three treatments. The two are
separate pieces of code, each with its own rule and its own callback. With no
treatment the management model should be the base model. Mapping a cell to the
base model's layers states that exactly. The parameters map by name, which is
the default.

The base model has a callback of its own, and each callback belongs to its own
model, so the map does not carry one across. `callback=` names the codomain's:

```{julia}
management, base = build(:eab_management), build(:emerald_ash_borer)
layers = Tuple(s.name for s in base.states)
reduce_to_base = ModelMap(management, base, c -> NamedTuple{layers}(c))
map((:none, :girdling, :insecticide, :ash_reduction)) do treatment
    prob = problem(:eab_management; n=60, years=12, treatment)
    (; treatment, is_map=is_model_map(reduce_to_base, prob; callback=eab_callback()))
end
```

Without treatment the two programs agree exactly at every saved state of a
twelve-year spread, including a callback that disperses beetles across the whole
landscape. Each treatment breaks the map, as it should.

The stress bias shows why the two checks differ. It changes only how beetles
disperse, in the callback, and the rule never reads it. The local check, given
cell states from a real run, sees nothing wrong, and only running the problem
exposes the difference:

```{julia}
biased = problem(:eab_management; n=60, years=12, stress_bias=true)
seen = solve(biased).u
all_layers = keys(seen[1])
cells = unique(reduce(vcat,
                      [vec(map((xs...) -> NamedTuple{all_layers}(xs), values(u)...))
                       for u in seen]))
(cell_states=length(cells),
 rules_commute=is_model_map(reduce_to_base; cells, p=biased.p, samples=5000),
 the_run_commutes=is_model_map(reduce_to_base, biased; callback=eab_callback()))
```

## Percolation inside a viral front

The multicomponent Domany–Kinzel model of a viral front [@Capitan2011] gives
each cell a replicative ability `r` in `0:R`. Its documentation says that
without mutation, and with every cell at `R`, it is directed bond percolation.
As a map, that claim has content: `r ↦ R r` sends the model with `R = 1` into the
model with `R`, provided that the resistance is rescaled. A cell with `n`
offspring resists with probability `π^n`, and multiplying abilities by `R`
multiplies `n` by `R`, so `π` must become `π^(1/R)`. The parameter map does the
work:

```{julia}
map((2, 3, 6)) do R
    bond, front = build_domany_kinzel_viral(; R=1), build_domany_kinzel_viral(; R)
    embed = ModelMap(bond, front, r -> Int8(R * r);
                     parameters=p -> (π=p.π^(1 / R), p=0.0, q=0.0))
    still = (π=0.3, p=0.0, q=0.0)
    prob = CAProblem(bond, (; r=Int8(1)), 400, still; space=Torus(500), seed=3)
    (; R, without_mutation=is_model_map(embed; p=still, contexts=2000, dims=1),
     with_mutation=is_model_map(embed; p=(π=0.3, p=0.2, q=0.0), contexts=2000, dims=1),
     a_run=is_model_map(embed, prob))
end
```

These are checks of the random numbers at 2000 contexts and over one run, not a
proof. The proof is the algebra above, up to rounding: `π^n` and
`(π^(1/R))^(R n)` can differ in their last bits, so a draw could in principle fall
between them, though that has a chance of order `10^-16` per draw.

## Quotients of models with callbacks

Fourteen of the zoo's models do much of their work in callbacks: decisions on the
whole lattice, dispersal, individuals acting one at a time. A callback reads the
whole state, so forgetting a layer needs a callback for the smaller state, and
`callback=:lift` builds it. After each step the state is lifted, with the
forgotten layer at its default, the original callback acts on the lifted state,
and the result is mapped down. The Lean library proves the construction: it
commutes exactly when the callback does not depend on what is forgotten, and it
is then the only callback that does (`Lumping.liftCallback`,
`Lumping.callback_unique`, `Lumping.runWith_quotient`). Whether that holds for a
given model is what running it tells us:

```{julia}
function forgets(id, layer; kw=(;))
    return (model=id, layer, setting=join(("$k=$v" for (k, v) in pairs(kw) if k != :n), ", "),
            is_map=is_model_map(forget_layers(build(id), layer), problem(id; kw...);
                                callback=:lift))
end
[forgets(:cassava_mealybug, :loss), forgets(:cassava_mealybug, :since),
 forgets(:potato_moth_farmers, :source), forgets(:potato_moth_farmers, :carriers),
 forgets(:western_x_orchard, :age), forgets(:western_x_orchard, :clock),
 forgets(:eab_management, :large; kw=(; n=40)),
 forgets(:eab_management, :large; kw=(; n=40, treatment=:girdling)),
 forgets(:eab_management, :phloem0; kw=(; n=40)),
 forgets(:eab_management, :phloem0; kw=(; n=40, stress_bias=true))]
```

Each `true` has a reason in the model's code. The mealybug's `loss` is written by
the rule and read only by a summary of the yield. The potato moth's `source`, the
origin of a cell's moths, is the published counterpart of the lineage label in
the previous vignette: it is copied from a neighbour or set when a farmer's team
brings moths in, and it never decides anything.
In the western X orchard, `age` sets yields and costs in the economic summary
but not the epidemic. The ash borer's layers show that the answer belongs to the
problem as well as the model: `large` matters once there is a treatment, and
`phloem0` only under the stress bias.

## A block rule: enemies that cannot catch anything

The three-layer Bt crop model is a block rule [@Yang2009], solved with the Margolus
scheme: pests and their enemies move in 2 × 2 blocks over a plant layer. Its
quotient is a block rule too, lifting a block and mapping the new block down.
None of its nine layers can be forgotten alone, but all four enemy layers can be
forgotten together when enemies cannot catch anything. Then they never touch the
pests, though they are there at the start and only later starve:

```{julia}
bt = build(:bt_crop_three_layer)
no_enemies = forget_layers(bt, :enemy, :enemy_age, :enemy_hunger, :enemy_genome)
map(((; P_DB=0.6, P_DC=0.6), (; P_DB=0.0, P_DC=0.0))) do predation
    prob = problem(:bt_crop_three_layer; pmap=predation)
    (; predation, enemies_at_start=count(prob.u0.enemy),
     is_map=is_model_map(no_enemies, prob; alg=Margolus()))
end
```

## A short run can hide a dependence

A `false` disproves a map, but a `true` holds only for the problem and the span
that was run. The grapevine leafroll model has an `age` layer, and forgetting it
looks harmless at first:

```{julia}
vine = problem(:grapevine_leafroll)
forget_age = forget_layers(build(:grapevine_leafroll), :age)
full = solve(vine)
down = solve(pushforward(forget_age, vine; callback=:lift))
(first_month_that_differs=full.t[findfirst(i -> pushforward(forget_age, full.u[i]) !=
                                                down.u[i], eachindex(full.u))],
 months=vine.tspan[2],
 is_map_over=map(T -> T => is_model_map(forget_age, remake(vine; tspan=(0, T));
                                        callback=:lift), (40, 60, 100, 600)))
```

How long an exposed vine takes to become infective depends on whether it is
younger than 60 months, and the lift makes every vine a new one, so the two runs
agree until the first vines come of age. No run shorter than that could tell
them apart.

## A layer used only within a step

Some layers matter within a step and not between steps. The ash borer's `larvae1`
is written by the rule and read by the callback in the same step, and the next
rule overwrites it without reading it, so what a saved state holds in that layer
is never used. Even so, a lifted callback cannot forget it. It maps down between
the rule and the callback, so the larvae are gone before the callback can see
them.

`callback=:lift_step` treats the rule and the callback as one step: it lifts the
state, runs the original's whole step, and maps the result down. Every step
starts from the lift rather than from where the original's last step ended, so
what is forgotten cannot be carried along, and a layer that matters still fails.
The first check below compares the two constructions:

```{julia}
function both_ways(id, layer; kw=(;))
    f, prob = forget_layers(build(id), layer), problem(id; kw...)
    return (model=id, layer, setting=join(("$k=$v" for (k, v) in pairs(kw) if k != :n), ", "),
            lifted_callback=is_model_map(f, prob; callback=:lift),
            whole_step=is_model_map(f, prob; callback=:lift_step))
end
[both_ways(:emerald_ash_borer, :larvae1; kw=(; n=41)),
 both_ways(:eab_management, :larvae1; kw=(; n=40)),
 both_ways(:eab_management, :larvae1; kw=(; n=40, treatment=:girdling)),
 both_ways(:eab_management, :larvae1; kw=(; n=40, stress_bias=true)),
 both_ways(:emerald_ash_borer, :adults; kw=(; n=41)),
 both_ways(:eab_management, :phloem0; kw=(; n=40)),
 both_ways(:eab_management, :phloem0; kw=(; n=40, stress_bias=true))]
```

Forgetting `larvae1` is a map in both models, with or without a treatment. It is
not vacuous, since the layer holds millions of larvae in the saved states, and the
smaller model does without them. Its rule commutes too, so the callback alone is
what the lifted construction trips over:

```{julia}
borer = problem(:emerald_ash_borer; n=41)
no_larvae1 = forget_layers(build(:emerald_ash_borer), :larvae1)
borer_run = solve(borer).u
borer_layers = keys(borer_run[1])
borer_cells = unique(reduce(vcat,
                            [vec(map((xs...) -> NamedTuple{borer_layers}(xs), values(u)...))
                             for u in borer_run]))
(peak_larvae1=maximum(u -> sum(u.larvae1), borer_run),
 layers_left=keys(solve(pushforward(no_larvae1, borer; callback=:lift_step)).u[end]),
 rules_commute=is_model_map(no_larvae1; cells=borer_cells, p=borer.p, samples=5000))
```

The whole step does not hide a dependence: `adults` still fails, and so does
`phloem0` under the stress bias, where the callback really reads it between
steps. Where a lifted callback works the two constructions are the same, so its
answers carry over.

The Lean library proves these relations. The
quotient runs every run of the original when the whole step does not depend on
what is forgotten, and it is then the only whole step that does
(`Lumping.runWith_wholeStep_quotient`, `Lumping.wholeStep_unique`). When the
rule and callback pass separately, lifting the whole step gives the same thing
as the lifted callback (`Lumping.wholeStep_descends`,
`Lumping.liftCallback_wholeStep`). And the whole step is strictly more general: a
small model has a rule and a whole step that can forget a layer while its callback
cannot, which is the shape of the larvae here (`wholeStep_strictly_more`).

Trying every layer of the zoo's layered models one at a time, 101 layers in 20
models at their usual settings with some of the long runs shortened, these two
`larvae1` layers are the only answers that change. Every layer that passed with a
lifted callback passed with the whole step too.

## What a quotient cannot express

Some limits remain:

- The problem that `callback=:lift_step` builds runs the original's whole step and
  has no local rule of its own, so it can be solved but not checked cell by cell.
- A layer that never leaves its default passes vacuously. `rogued` and `tested`
  in the grapevine model are like that at its default settings, which says
  nothing about the runs that use them.
- Event rules, which give rates rather than a next state, are refused by
  `quotient`.
- A callback may refuse to run on what is left. Forgetting `farmers` in the potato
  moth model raises the model's own error, and that is an answer too.
- The dune model with `speedup = 0` is not an example: it is one model at another
  parameter value, not a second model.

## Summary

| relation | check | result |
|---|---|---|
| *Tuta* forgetting its record layers | run, 300 months on real climate | a map |
| *Tuta* forgetting `land` | run | not a map |
| ash borer management, no treatment → base model | run, with the base model's callback | a map |
| ash borer management, any treatment → base model | run | not a map |
| ash borer management, stress bias → base model | rules; run | rules commute, the run does not |
| viral front `R = 1` → `R`, no mutation, `π ↦ π^(1/R)` | rules at 2000 contexts; run | a map |
| the same, with mutation | rules | not a map |
| mealybug without `loss`, potato moth without `source`, orchard without `age` | run, lifted callback | a map |
| Bt crop without its enemy layers, no predation | run, block rule | a map |
| the same, with predation | run, block rule | not a map |
| grapevine without `age` | run, lifted callback | not a map, from month 61 |
| ash borer without `larvae1` | run, lifted callback | not a map: read between rule and callback |
| the same | rules; run, whole step | rules commute, and a map |
| ash borer without `adults` | run, whole step | not a map |
